content: Several key figures in the free and open-source software community, including Linus Torvalds, Larry Wall, Brian Behlendorf, Eric Allman, Guido van Rossum, Michael Tiemann, Paul Vixie, Jamie Zawinski of Netscape, and Eric Raymond, convened to address the confusion surrounding the term free software. During this meeting, the developers voted on a new term, and the result was announced at a press conference later that evening. Five days after the meeting, Eric Raymond publicly called on the free software community to adopt the new term. This led to the formation of the Open Source Initiative (OSI) in February 1998 by Raymond and Bruce Perens. The OSI leveraged approximately two decades of evidence from case studies of both closed and open development models, as observed on the Internet, to advocate for the adoption of open-source practices by commercial businesses. Their goal was to highlight the practical benefits of freely available source code and to encourage major software companies and high-tech industries to embrace open-source principles. Bruce Perens adapted Debian's Free Software Guidelines to create the Open Source Definition. Open-source software (OSS) projects are developed and maintained by networks of volunteer programmers. Prominent examples of open-source products include the Apache HTTP Server, the Internet Protocol (IP) address system, and the Mozilla Firefox web browser. Among these, the Linux operating system stands out as one of the most successful open-source projects. Linux is a Unix-like operating system that is entirely open source. Criticism of the Open Source Initiative (OSI) principles often revolves around their differentiation from other terms and definitions, such as those related to patents or trademarks that may disadvantage individual contributors or creators. Another critique of the open-source movement is the claim that these projects are not as self-organizing as proponents suggest. Critics argue that successful open-source projects often rely on strong central management, even if the manager is a volunteer. Chuck Connell's article, Open Source Projects Manage Themselves? Dream On, elaborates on this perspective. However, this critique targets the development model rather than the concept of open source itself. The author does not assert that self-organization is inherently ineffective but highlights cases where central management likely played a role. Legal and cultural criticisms of open source are often addressed as part of broader objections by those who favor share-alike principles, such as those endorsed by Creative Commons. Creative Commons licenses, such as CC-BY-NC-SA (Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike), often conflict with OSI principles. Richard Stallman of the Free Software Foundation (FSF), whose GNU Free Documentation License (GFDL) is used by Wikipedia, opposes the use of the term open source to describe what he refers to as free software. While legally, free software qualifies as open source, Stallman considers the categorization to be misleading. He also opposes the pragmatic approach of the OSI, fearing that it compromises the FSF's idealistic standards of software freedom, which emphasize freedom and community. There are several recognized barriers to the adoption of open-source software by enterprises. These include concerns about the viral nature of open-source licenses, the lack of formal support and training, the rapid pace of change, and the absence of a long-term roadmap. Most of these barriers are related to perceived risks. However, it is worth noting that not all proprietary projects disclose their future plans, not all open-source licenses are equally viral, and many serious OSS projects, particularly operating systems, generate revenue through paid support and documentation. Various business models have emerged around open-source software to mitigate these risks and provide a whole product solution. This whole product typically includes support, commercial licenses, professional services, training, certification, partner programs, references, and use cases. These business models range from services-only organizations that do not contribute to software development to models where the majority of the software is created by full-time developers employed by a central organization. These models are relatively new and not widely understood. One such model is the Bee Keeper Model. A commonly employed business strategy among commercial open-source software firms is the dual-license strategy, as exemplified by companies like MySQL and Alfresco.
